To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adaptation effects for timbre are found in the absence of acoustic overlap between the adaptor and test series and in the presence of cross-ear presentation.

(1) the results of the present study provide evidence for an intermediate stage in the processing of timbre that is analogous to the second-stage representation proposed in the literature on speech perception, (2) the results of our study provide evidence for a central representation in the processing of instrument timbre, (3) the results of all the experiments in our study are consistent with the proposal that the central representation of timbre is abstract, (4) the results of two experiments in our study provide evidence that
adaptation to the timbre of the trumpet yielded an abstract representation of the continuum, and this abstract representation was similar to that of phonemes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the auditory system represents the sounds of the world.
the question of how we process the sounds of speech and music and how these processes might be related.
the representation of the acoustic attributes of speech sounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there are two levels of processing in the perception of timbre: one level that is sensitive to the physical attributes of the stimulus (e.g., the frequency of a tone), and another that is sensitive to abstract attributes (e.g., timbre).
the results are compatible with an abstract encoding of timbre, and that this is a second stage of processing.
the perceptual system is organized to encode the abstract attributes of sounds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
timbre perception is a two-stage process.
timbre, like phonetics, can be encoded at an abstract level.
the abstract encoding of timbre is similar to that of speech sounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the abstract timbre representation is a central one.
the abstract representation of instrument timbres is a central representation, and that this is true of both phonetic and nonphonetic stimuli.
timbre is encoded in a central representation that is abstract, categorical, and independent of acoustic properties of the stimuli.
